metaDescription: User-generated content is content your customers make about you. How to collect it legally, where it converts hardest, and the rights you need first.
definition: User-generated content is content about a brand created by its customers rather than by the brand — reviews, photos, unboxing videos, comparison posts.
answer: User-generated content is content your customers make about you — reviews, photos, unboxing videos — that you didn't pay for. Paid "UGC-style" creator content looks identical and isn't the same thing: it's an ad, and Indian disclosure rules apply. Either way, you need written permission before it runs in a campaign.
takeaways: **Organic UGC and paid UGC-style content are different products.** Calling the second one the first is where brands get into trouble.
A reshare inside the app is not a licence. Copyright in the photo sits with whoever shot it.
Permission needs to name the asset, the channels, the duration and whether it will run as paid media.
UGC converts hardest where doubt is highest: the product page, right next to the buy button.

sections.h2: Organic UGC versus paid UGC-style content
body: The line gets blurred constantly, usually without anyone meaning to mislead.

**Organic UGC** is unpaid and unprompted. A customer photographs the sofa in their living room, posts it, tags you. Its power comes entirely from the fact that it wasn't bought — and evaporates the moment it turns out it was.

**Paid UGC-style content** is a production service: you commission a creator, brief the hook, pay a fee, run the files as ads from your own handle. Often excellent performance creative, nothing wrong with using it. It just isn't social proof. Calling it "authentic customer content" is describing content you wrote.
The test: did money or free product change hands, and did you have editorial control? Yes to either and it's advertising.

sections.h2: Permission: what a reshare gets you, and what it doesn't
body: In India, copyright in a photograph or video belongs to whoever created it, under the Copyright Act, 1957. Posting it publicly doesn't transfer that to the brand it features, and tagging you isn't consent. Instagram's terms grant Instagram a licence — not you.

Resharing and reuse are different acts. Adding a tagged post to your story with the app's own function is the platform doing its job. Downloading the file and running it as paid media needs permission.
It rarely needs a lawyer. It does need to be written and specific — a DM reply is fine if it names four things:
bullets: **Which asset** — link the exact post, not "your recent photos".
**Which channels and for how long** — website, ads, print, in-store screens; six months, a year, perpetual. "Marketing, forever" gets refused.
**Whether it runs as paid media** — the one people object to afterwards.
**Whether identifiable people appear** — a face that isn't the poster's needs its own agreement.

callout.title: The expensive shortcut
callout.body: Pulling a hashtag feed straight onto your product pages with no human check is how a competitor's post or somebody's complaint ends up embedded next to your buy button. Automate the collection, never the approval.

body: There's no honest single uplift figure for UGC — the ones circulating in decks are usually a vendor's own sample. The mechanism is what's consistent: UGC answers the objection a studio shot structurally cannot.

A studio photo shows the product under perfect light in a perfect room. The buyer wants to know what it looks like in *their* living room, on their skin tone, at their size, after two washes. Only a customer photo answers that — which is why the best placement isn't the Instagram grid. It's the product page, next to the price and the buy button, where the hesitation happens.

Three others earn their keep: paid social, where UGC-style creative dodges the polish that signals "ad" to a scrolling thumb; photo reviews, which also feed [review management](/services/review-management-services); and the enquiry follow-up, where two customer videos beat a third discount.

sections.h2: How to get customers to make it
body: Most brands wait for UGC, decide their customers don't post, and stop. Usually nobody asked at the moment the customer was most pleased.
numbered: **Ask three to seven days after delivery**, not on dispatch — when the thing is in use and the novelty is fresh. WhatsApp beats email for this.
**Put the ask on the packaging** — an insert card with a short [branded hashtag](/glossary/hashtags) and a QR code costs a few rupees.
**Make it specific.** "Show us where you put it" gets photos. "Share your experience" gets nothing.
**Reply to everyone who posts**, publicly and by name. People make the second post because the first got noticed.
**If you incentivise, disclose it.** A discount code for a post creates a material connection and the post needs a label — see [influencer marketing](/glossary/influencer-marketing-meaning).

sections.h2: Moderation, and the day it goes wrong
body: Every collection mechanism eventually collects something you didn't want. Tags get hijacked, and a customer with a genuine complaint uses the same tag as everyone else.

Keep a human in the loop before publication, file permission emails with the assets so you can prove consent a year later, and honour a takedown request the day it arrives even if your paperwork is watertight. Arguing with a customer about a licence costs more than the asset.
When the tag surfaces a complaint instead of a compliment, treat it as information. That's [social listening](/glossary/social-listening), and it's usually worth more than the photo you wanted.

faqs.q: What does UGC mean in marketing?
faqs.a: User-generated content: content about your brand made by customers rather than by you. In practice the term now covers two different things — genuine unpaid customer content, and paid creator content shot to look like it. Worth being precise about which one you're buying.

faqs.q: Do I need permission to repost a customer's photo?
faqs.a: To reshare it inside the platform using its own function, generally no. To download it and use it on your website, in an ad, or in print, yes. Copyright stays with the person who shot it, and a tag isn't consent. Ask in writing and keep the reply.

Someone who makes UGC-style video for brands to run as ads, usually without posting it to their own account. It's a content production role, not an influencer role — you're buying the footage and the format, not their audience. Rates reflect that difference.

faqs.q: Is paid UGC allowed under Indian advertising rules?
faqs.a: Yes, provided it's disclosed where there's a material connection between the brand and the person posting. ASCI's influencer guidelines require a clear, upfront label. Content you commission and run yourself as a brand ad is plainly an ad; content posted from a creator's account needs the label.

faqs.q: Where should I put UGC on my website?
faqs.a: The product page, near the price and the add-to-cart button, where the hesitation actually happens. A gallery on a separate page looks tidy and does very little, because nobody navigates to a UGC gallery while deciding whether to buy.
